title: ATM
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, session state, chain-of-responsibility cash dispenser with plan-then-commit, runnable Java and Kotlin, account-level atomicity and idempotency, follow-ups.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design an ATM: insert card, enter PIN, check balance, withdraw cash.

Functional:

  • Card inserted, then PIN (3 wrong attempts ejects the card), then a session.
  • Balance enquiry and cash withdrawal in notes of 2000, 500 and 100.
  • Withdraw succeeds only if the account has enough money and the machine can make the exact amount from the notes it holds.
  • Notes leave the machine only after the account is debited.

Non-functional: the order of operations must never give free cash or take money without paying; the account is shared (many ATMs, apps).

Worked example. Account has 5,000. Withdraw 3,700 with notes 2000, 500, 100 available: plan = one 2000, three 500 (1500), two 100 (200) = 3,700. Debit leaves 1,300. A request for 150 fails because no combination of 100s makes it, and the account is NOT debited.

Industry examples. Real ATMs (NCR, Diebold Nixdorf) talk the ISO 8583 message protocol to the bank's switch; banks authorise and debit on their side, and the ATM dispenses only after approval. Indian UPI/IMPS back ends use idempotency keys so a retry after a network timeout never double-debits.

Everyday analogy. A shopkeeper who first checks the cash drawer can make the exact change, then takes your money, and only then hands over the goods.

Common interview traps.

  • Dispensing cash before the debit is confirmed (or debiting before checking the machine can pay).
  • Forgetting the PIN retry limit and card ejection.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• Account: id, PIN (a hash in real life), balance in minor units, debit and credit.
  • Bank: finds accounts; in reality a remote service (the ATM is a thin client).
  • NoteHandler chain and Dispenser: how cash is made.
  • ATM: session state (IDLE, CARD_IN, AUTHENTICATED) and the operations.

Plan, then commit. The dispenser first computes a plan (which notes) without changing anything, the account is debited, then the plan is committed to the cash counts. That order means a failed plan never costs the customer money, and a failed debit never loses cash. If the machine crashes between debit and dispense, a real ATM writes a journal and the bank reverses the transaction on reconciliation.

Decision gravity. The ATM is a thin client of the bank (the bank owns the balance): a one-way door you must keep, since money lives in one place. The dispenser's greedy algorithm (largest note first) is correct for canonical sets like 2000/500/100 but not for arbitrary denominations; changing to dynamic programming later is a local, reversible change.

Everyday analogy. A vending machine with a bank behind it: counts what it holds, asks the bank for permission, then dispenses.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing the PIN in plain text or logging it.
  • Money as double; use long in paise or cents.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing the cash-handling logic into the ATM class.
  • No state guard: calling withdraw before authentication.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• State (session). Operations are legal only in certain states. An enum plus a require(state) guard is enough here; a full State class per state is the same shape as the vending machine and can be used if the flow grows (PIN change, deposit).
  • Chain of Responsibility (notes). Each handler takes what it can and passes the rest. Why: adding a 200 note is one new handler. Alternative: a loop over a sorted list of denominations (shorter, equally good; say so).
  • Facade. ATM hides Bank, Dispenser and state.
  • Proxy/Adapter (optional). Bank is an interface to the remote core banking system.
  • Command/Memento for the journal (optional). Each transaction as an object so it can be logged and reversed.

Industry examples. Java servlet filters and Express/OkHttp interceptors are chains of responsibility. Payment systems (Stripe, Razorpay) use idempotency keys plus a transaction journal for exactly the crash window described above.

Everyday analogy. Paying with change: hand over the biggest bills first, then smaller ones for the rest.

Common interview traps.

  • Over-using patterns when a sorted list and a loop is clearer.
  • Greedy that fails on non-canonical denominations; state the assumption.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Java (compiled and run with JDK 21):

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

class Account {
    final String id; final String pin;
    protected long balance;
    Account(String id, String pin, long balance) { this.id = id; this.pin = pin; this.balance = balance; }
    long balance() { return balance; }
    /** Check-then-act: NOT safe when two ATMs hit the same account (see Concurrency). */
    boolean debit(long amt) {
        if (amt <= 0 || balance < amt) return false;
        balance -= amt; return true;
    }
    void credit(long amt) { balance += amt; }
}

class Bank {
    protected final Map<String, Account> accounts = new HashMap<>();
    void add(Account a) { accounts.put(a.id, a); }
    Account find(String id) { return accounts.get(id); }
}

/** Chain of Responsibility: each handler dispenses as many notes of its value as it can, then passes the rest on. */
abstract class NoteHandler {
    final int value; int count; NoteHandler next;
    NoteHandler(int value, int count) { this.value = value; this.count = count; }
    /** Plan only (no mutation): fills `out` and returns true if exact amount can be made. */
    boolean plan(long amt, Map<Integer, Integer> out) {
        int use = (int) Math.min(count, amt / value);
        long rest = amt - (long) use * value;
        if (use > 0) out.put(value, use);
        if (rest == 0) return true;
        return next != null && next.plan(rest, out);
    }
    void commit(Map<Integer, Integer> plan) {
        count -= plan.getOrDefault(value, 0);
        if (next != null) next.commit(plan);
    }
}
class Notes extends NoteHandler { Notes(int v, int c) { super(v, c); } }

class Dispenser {
    private final NoteHandler head;
    Dispenser(NoteHandler... hs) {                    // pass the biggest note first
        for (int i = 0; i + 1 < hs.length; i++) hs[i].next = hs[i + 1];
        head = hs[0];
    }
    Optional<Map<Integer, Integer>> plan(long amt) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> out = new TreeMap<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
        return head.plan(amt, out) ? Optional.of(out) : Optional.empty();
    }
    void commit(Map<Integer, Integer> p) { head.commit(p); }
}

enum AtmState { IDLE, CARD_IN, AUTHENTICATED }

class ATM {
    private final Bank bank; private final Dispenser cash;
    private AtmState state = AtmState.IDLE;
    private Account current; private int badPins = 0;

    ATM(Bank bank, Dispenser cash) { this.bank = bank; this.cash = cash; }

    void insertCard(String accountId) {
        require(AtmState.IDLE);
        current = bank.find(accountId);
        if (current == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown card");
        state = AtmState.CARD_IN; badPins = 0;
    }
    boolean enterPin(String pin) {
        require(AtmState.CARD_IN);
        if (current.pin.equals(pin)) { state = AtmState.AUTHENTICATED; return true; }
        if (++badPins >= 3) eject();                  // swallow/eject after 3 tries
        return false;
    }
    long balance() { require(AtmState.AUTHENTICATED); return current.balance(); }

    Map<Integer, Integer> withdraw(long amt) {
        require(AtmState.AUTHENTICATED);
        Map<Integer, Integer> plan = cash.plan(amt)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("ATM cannot make " + amt));
        if (!current.debit(amt)) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
        cash.commit(plan);                            // notes leave only after the debit succeeded
        return plan;
    }
    void eject() { state = AtmState.IDLE; current = null; }
    AtmState state() { return state; }
    private void require(AtmState s) { if (state != s) throw new IllegalStateException("state is " + state + ", need " + s); }
}

Kotlin core (hand translated, not compiled in this session):

class Account(val id: String, private val pin: String, private var balance: Long) {
    @Synchronized fun balance() = balance
    @Synchronized fun debit(amt: Long): Boolean {
        if (amt <= 0 || balance < amt) return false
        balance -= amt; return true
    }
    fun pinOk(p: String) = pin == p
}

/** Greedy plan, largest note first; returns null if the exact amount cannot be made. */
class Dispenser(private val notes: MutableMap<Int, Int>) {       // note value -> count, e.g. 2000 to 10
    fun plan(amt: Long): Map<Int, Int>? {
        var rest = amt
        val out = linkedMapOf<Int, Int>()
        for ((value, count) in notes.toSortedMap(reverseOrder())) {
            val use = minOf(count.toLong(), rest / value).toInt()
            if (use > 0) { out[value] = use; rest -= use.toLong() * value }
        }
        return if (rest == 0L) out else null
    }
    fun commit(plan: Map<Int, Int>) = plan.forEach { (v, n) -> notes[v] = notes.getValue(v) - n }
}

enum class AtmState { IDLE, CARD_IN, AUTHENTICATED }

class Atm(private val accounts: Map<String, Account>, private val cash: Dispenser) {
    var state = AtmState.IDLE; private set
    private var current: Account? = null

    fun withdraw(amt: Long): Map<Int, Int> {
        check(state == AtmState.AUTHENTICATED) { "not authenticated" }
        val plan = cash.plan(amt) ?: error("ATM cannot make $amt")
        check(current!!.debit(amt)) { "insufficient funds" }
        cash.commit(plan)                                  // notes leave only after the debit
        return plan
    }
}

Choices: plan does not mutate, so it can be retried; the greedy chain returns "cannot make" for 150 because only 100s are left. The PIN is compared as a plain string for brevity only; production stores a salted hash and the bank verifies it (the ATM never knows it).

Common interview traps.

  • Mutating note counts during planning, then failing halfway and leaving the machine inconsistent.
  • Allowing debit(0) or negative amounts.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Bank bank = new Bank();
        bank.add(new SafeAccount("acc1", "1234", 5_000));
        Dispenser cash = new Dispenser(new Notes(2000, 10), new Notes(500, 10), new Notes(100, 10));
        ATM atm = new ATM(bank, cash);
        atm.insertCard("acc1");
        System.out.println("wrong pin ok? " + atm.enterPin("0000"));      // false
        System.out.println("right pin ok? " + atm.enterPin("1234"));      // true
        System.out.println("notes for 3700 = " + atm.withdraw(3700));     // {2000=1, 500=3, 100=2}
        System.out.println("balance = " + atm.balance());                  // 1300
        try { atm.withdraw(150); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("error: " + e.getMessage()); }
        atm.eject();

        // 10 ATMs, same account with 1000, each withdraws 200: exactly 5 may succeed
        Account shared = new SafeAccount("acc2", "1", 1_000);
        ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);
        CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1);
        List<Future<Boolean>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) fs.add(ex.submit(() -> { go.await(); return shared.debit(200); }));
        go.countDown();
        int ok = 0; for (Future<Boolean> f : fs) if (f.get()) ok++;
        ex.shutdown();
        System.out.println("successful = " + ok + ", balance = " + shared.balance());   // 5, 0
    }
}

Actual output from javac Demo.java && java Demo:

wrong pin ok? false
right pin ok? true
notes for 3700 = {2000=1, 500=3, 100=2}
balance = 1300
error: ATM cannot make 150
successful = 5, balance = 0

The last line is the concurrency test: ten threads each withdraw 200 from 1,000; exactly five succeed and the balance ends at 0, never negative.

Common interview traps.

  • Not testing: wrong PIN thrice, not enough cash in machine, not enough balance, withdraw before login.
  • Asserting only the happy path.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
The shared resource is the account, not the ATM. The same account can be debited from several ATMs, a mobile app and an auto-debit at the same time. debit is check-then-act: it reads balance >= amt, then subtracts. Two threads with balance 1,000 and amt 800 can both pass the check and drive the balance to -600.

Fix options, with gravity:

  1. synchronized on the account (below): correct inside one JVM, trivial to reason about.
  2. AtomicLong with a compare-and-set loop: lock-free on a single value.
  3. Database: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ? and check that one row changed; or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in a transaction. This is the real answer, because the account lives in a database shared by many servers, where JVM locks do nothing.
class SafeAccount extends Account {
    SafeAccount(String id, String pin, long bal) { super(id, pin, bal); }
    @Override synchronized boolean debit(long amt) { return super.debit(amt); }   // check + subtract together
    @Override synchronized void credit(long amt) { super.credit(amt); }
    @Override synchronized long balance() { return super.balance(); }
}
// Cash in a real ATM is one physical machine with one user, so Dispenser needs no lock.
// The shared thing is the ACCOUNT (many ATMs, mobile app, UPI): that is where the lock (or a DB row lock) lives.

Idempotency. If the ATM times out after sending a debit, it does not know whether it happened. Give each withdrawal a unique transaction id; the bank stores processed ids and returns the original result on a retry, so a retry never debits twice.

Symptom in production. Negative balances or a customer debited with no cash dispensed. Metrics: accounts with balance < 0, count of debits with no matching dispense in the journal.

Everyday analogy. Two cashiers drawing from the same till: each must look at the till and take cash in one uninterrupted motion.

Common interview traps.

  • Locking the ATM but not the account.
  • Synchronising in Java and thinking it works across servers.
  • Locking two accounts in different orders for a transfer (deadlock); order locks by account id.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Deposit and transfer. Transfers lock two accounts in id order, or do both updates in one DB transaction.
  • Daily withdrawal limit. Another check in withdraw; store the day's total on the account.
  • Denominations that are not canonical. Replace greedy with a bounded coin-change DP.
  • Out-of-cash and fraud. An OUT_OF_SERVICE state; velocity checks at the bank.
  • Receipts and audit log. A journal written before dispensing, replayed on restart.
  • Security. PIN as a hash verified by the bank; encrypted PIN block; lock after 3 attempts.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "how to scale" with locks; across servers the answer is the database's atomicity plus idempotency.
  • Ignoring the crash window between debit and dispense.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Flow: insert card, PIN (3 tries), authenticated session, operations, eject. Session guarded by an enum state.
  • Cash dispensing is a chain of handlers with a plan-then-commit order; debit happens between plan and commit.
  • Money is an integer in minor units; PIN is never stored in plain text in real systems.
  • Concurrency: the shared object is the account; make check-and-subtract atomic (lock in a JVM, conditional UPDATE in a database) and make retries idempotent.
  • Extensions: transfers (lock ordering), limits, non-canonical notes (DP), audit journal.

questions.promptHtml: In an ATM withdrawal, why do we compute which notes to give, then debit the account, and only then reduce the machine's note counts? Why not just debit first?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you reason about the order of side effects so that no failure leaves free cash or a lost debit.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I split the work into three steps: plan (pure calculation, changes nothing), debit (the one step that can legitimately fail on funds), and commit (reduce note counts, dispense). If the plan fails, the customer was never charged. If the debit fails, the machine never lost cash. The only bad window left is a crash between debit and dispense, which a journal and bank reconciliation cover.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each step can fail for a different reason:

Plan   : fails if the machine cannot make the exact amount   (no side effect)
Debit  : fails if balance < amount                           (side effect at the bank)
Commit : reduce counts, physically dispense                  (side effect on the machine)

Put the step with no side effect first, then the step that is hardest to undo (money at the bank), and the mechanical step last. If we debit first and the plan then fails (150 cannot be made from 100s only... or the machine is short of 500s), we must refund, which is another operation that can itself fail. Plan is also retryable because it does not mutate counts.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Map<Integer,Integer> plan = cash.plan(amt).orElseThrow();   // 1. no mutation
if (!current.debit(amt)) throw new IllegalStateException(); // 2. money moves
cash.commit(plan);                                          // 3. counts change, notes leave
val plan = cash.plan(amt) ?: error("cannot make $amt")   // 1. no mutation
check(current!!.debit(amt)) { "insufficient funds" }     // 2. money moves
cash.commit(plan)                                        // 3. counts change, notes leave

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Debiting first and refunding on plan failure (two writes, refund can fail too).
  • Mutating note counts inside the plan so a half-failed plan corrupts the machine.
  • Thinking the order removes every failure: a crash after debit but before dispense still needs a journal.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the machine crashes after the debit? -> Write a journal entry before dispensing; on restart or at reconciliation the bank reverses any debit with no dispense event.
  2. Why must plan not mutate? -> So a failed or retried plan leaves the machine unchanged and idempotent.
  3. Why is the ATM a thin client of the bank? -> The balance must live in one place; the ATM only requests authorisation and dispenses after approval.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "check balance, then dispense". The senior names each step's failure mode, orders by reversibility, and names the residual crash window with its journal fix.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Real ATMs dispense only after the bank's approval message and keep a transaction journal for exactly the debited-but-not-dispensed disputes.

questions.promptHtml: The cash dispenser is a chain of handlers (2000, 500, 100). Is that better than a loop over a sorted list of denominations, and when does the greedy approach give a wrong answer?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks you can justify a pattern honestly (not pattern-stuffing) and know the limits of greedy.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Both work; the chain makes adding a new note a one-class change, the loop is shorter. I would say that honestly and pick the loop unless the interviewer wants the pattern. Separately, greedy (largest note first) is only safe for canonical note sets with enough of each note. With limited counts or odd denominations it can say "cannot make it" when an answer exists, and then you need bounded coin-change DP.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Chain: each handler takes min(count, amt / value) of its note and passes the remainder on. Loop: same logic over sorted(values, desc).

Where greedy fails, with limited stock: machine holds one 500 and three 200s, no 100s. Ask for 600.

greedy : 500 x1 -> rest 100 -> 200 cannot make 100 -> FAIL
correct: 200 x3 = 600

Fix: bounded coin-change DP over (note, count) states, or backtracking; the amounts and note types are tiny so cost is negligible. Because plan is behind the Dispenser interface, this is a local, reversible change.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming greedy is always correct.
  • Adding handlers, factories and builders for three denominations.
  • Forgetting the plan needs the machine's current counts, not just face values.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you add a 200 note? -> Chain: new handler inserted; loop: add to the map.
  2. What is the complexity of DP here? -> O(amount/gcd * notes) with bounds; amounts are small.
  3. How would you prefer to dispense, big notes or balanced? -> A policy: balance cassettes so none runs out first; that is another reason to keep planning separate.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer praises the pattern. The senior states the trade-off, then names the greedy failure with a concrete stock example.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A machine reported "cannot dispense" for 600 while holding plenty of cash; greedy on a short 100 cassette was the cause.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate sends this withdraw for review. The ATM holds 10 notes each of 2000, 500, 100. The account has 5,000.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Map<Integer,Integer> withdraw(long amt) {
    require(AtmState.AUTHENTICATED);
    Map<Integer,Integer> plan = new TreeMap<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
    long rest = amt;
    for (NoteHandler h : handlers) {
        int use = (int) Math.min(h.count, rest / h.value);
        h.count -= use;                       // take notes now
        if (use > 0) plan.put(h.value, use);
        rest -= (long) use * h.value;
    }
    if (rest != 0) throw new IllegalStateException("cannot make " + amt);
    if (!current.debit(amt)) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
    return plan;
}
fun withdraw(amt: Long): Map<Int, Int> {
    check(state == AtmState.AUTHENTICATED)
    val plan = linkedMapOf<Int, Int>()
    var rest = amt
    for (h in handlers) {
        val use = minOf(h.count.toLong(), rest / h.value).toInt()
        h.count -= use                        // take notes now
        if (use > 0) plan[h.value] = use
        rest -= use.toLong() * h.value
    }
    check(rest == 0L) { "cannot make $amt" }
    check(current!!.debit(amt)) { "insufficient funds" }
    return plan
}

Testing 150 gives "cannot make 150". Testing 9,000 on the 5,000 account gives "insufficient funds".
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, what does the machine look like after those two failing calls, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, both errors are thrown." They miss that counts were mutated before either check passed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the dispenser used by one session at a time (yes, one physical machine)? Do we have a journal? Is there a test for failure paths?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident, so I stop the merge. If it shipped, I would take the machine out of service because its in-memory counts no longer match the cassettes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) planning mutates state (the line h.count -= use); (b) 9,000 request: notes are taken for 5,000+ then the debit fails; (c) no commit step, so counts are reduced even if nothing is dispensed.
  4. How I'd verify: Unit test: call withdraw(150) then assert counts unchanged; call withdraw(9000) and assert counts unchanged. Both fail on this code (the 150 case leaves 2000/500/100 notes taken).
  5. Root cause: Plan and commit are fused. Failure after the mutation leaves the machine believing it gave away notes it still holds.
  6. Fix: Plan is a read-only computation returning the map; debit; then commit(plan) reduces counts (see the reference code). Short term, copy counts into a local array during planning.
  7. Prevention: Failure-path tests (cannot make, insufficient funds, wrong state) asserting counts unchanged; code review rule: no mutation before the last check.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add a rollback that adds the notes back; rollback code is its own bug source. Not mutating is simpler.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if two threads call withdraw? -> One physical machine, one user at a time; the shared object is the account, not the dispenser.
  • Debit succeeds but the commit throws? -> Journal first; bank reverses unmatched debits.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A kiosk reported "out of 500s" after a day of declined requests; each declined request had quietly subtracted notes from the counter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves the code.
  • Hire: spots mutation before checks and proposes plan then commit.
  • Strong hire: also writes the failure-path tests, mentions the debit/dispense crash window and the journal.

questions.contextHtml: The ATM works with 2000, 500, 100 notes. Product now asks for two changes in the same sprint: (1) add a 200-note cassette in some machines, (2) a daily withdrawal limit of 20,000 per account, resetting at midnight. Rollout is across 40,000 machines with different cassette sets, and the account balance lives in the bank service.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change, which do not, and where does the limit live?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Edits the ATM class with new if branches for both, putting the limit in the ATM's memory.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the limit per account across all channels (ATM, UPI) or per card? Which timezone is midnight? Does a failed attempt count? Is the 200 note a priority or just an extra cassette?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; I would ship the 200 note first because it is isolated.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (design options): (a) limit in the ATM: wrong, 40,000 machines each have a partial view; (b) limit in the Account/bank: correct, because it is shared state; (c) a separate LimitPolicy object the bank applies.
  4. How I'd verify: Tests: 200 handler placed between 500 and 100 and then 700 is dispensed as 500+200; limit tests using an injected clock, two machines, same account.
  5. Root cause of the design answer: 200 note = new NoteHandler instance, with the order passed to Dispenser, so ATM, Account, Bank do not change (open/closed). The limit changes debit (or a bank-side policy) because only the account's owner can see all channels.
  6. Fix: Add dailyWithdrawn and lastDay to the account (or the bank's ledger), check dailyWithdrawn + amt <= limit inside the same atomic operation as the balance check so two ATMs cannot both pass.
  7. Prevention: Make the limit configurable per account type; add tests with a fake clock at 23:59:59 and 00:00:00.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not keep counters in the ATM or a cache without atomic update; and not store the limit in a global static.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Limit differs for premium cards? -> Strategy: LimitPolicy looked up by account type.
  • Midnight in which zone? -> Account's home zone; store the day key, not elapsed hours.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A limit enforced in a mobile app but not in the switch was bypassed by calling the ATM channel; the rule moved into the bank's debit path.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: if/else in ATM; limit local to the machine.
  • Hire: new handler, limit on the account.
  • Strong hire: limit checked atomically with the balance check, clock injection, per-account policy.

questions.contextHtml:
A bank's ATM fleet (1,200 machines) plus a mobile app debit the same accounts. A reconciliation job reports 37 accounts with negative balances overnight. All affected accounts are salary accounts hit at the same minute by an auto-debit and an ATM withdrawal. Sample log for one account (balance 1,000):

10:00:00.012 atm-17  debit acc9 800  read balance=1000 ok
10:00:00.013 app-03  debit acc9 800  read balance=1000 ok
10:00:00.014 atm-17  write balance=200
10:00:00.015 app-03  write balance=200   (or -600 on a read-modify-write variant)

The service runs 6 JVM instances with the Account.debit shown in the notes (check, then subtract).
questions.promptHtml: Explain the cause and give the fix. Would synchronized be enough?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add synchronized to debit." That fixes one JVM only; six instances still race.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where is the balance stored (DB or in memory)? Same row for all channels? Are retries possible? Is the isolation level read committed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block debits on affected accounts, alert, and let reconciliation reverse overdrafts per policy.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) check-then-act without atomicity; (b) multiple instances, so JVM locks do nothing; (c) a retry applied twice (the idempotency gap); red herring: clock skew between servers, since the same row serialises the writes regardless of time.
  4. How I'd verify: Query accounts with balance < 0; join the journal for debits with identical amounts within ms; reproduce with 10 threads and a latch, expecting more than 5 of 10 successes on 1,000 with 200 each.
  5. Root cause: The read and the write are two steps; two actors interleave between them.
  6. Fix: One atomic statement: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - :amt WHERE id = :id AND balance >= :amt and check rows affected = 1. Alternative: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a transaction. synchronized is fine only as a single-JVM demonstration.
  7. Prevention: A DB CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint as final guard, concurrency test with a latch, alert on negative balance.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a distributed lock service for this; the database row is already the arbiter. Not optimistic retry loops on hot salary accounts at month end.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 5,000 debits per second on one account? -> Row lock serialises; if it is a real hotspot, use a ledger of entries and aggregate, or queue per account.
  • AtomicLong? -> CAS works inside one JVM only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An overdraft bug appeared only on the 1st of the month when auto-debits and ATM cash-outs coincided; a unit test with two threads and a latch reproduced it in seconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: synchronized only.
  • Hire: conditional UPDATE or row lock and why JVM locks fail across servers.
  • Strong hire: also a CHECK constraint, idempotency, and a latch-based reproduction.

questions.contextHtml: You inherit an ATM class that creates new RemoteBank() and new CashDispenser() inside its constructor, reads System.currentTimeMillis() for the daily limit, and prints to console. A PIN lockout bug shipped: the card was ejected on the 4th wrong PIN instead of the 3rd. There are no tests.
questions.promptHtml: How would you make this testable and which tests would you write first?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Mockito to mock static methods." They never fix the hard-wired dependencies.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can I change constructors (yes, internal)? Is there an integration environment? Does the bank service have a sandbox?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin the lockout bug with a characterisation test before refactoring.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (why it is untestable): hard-wired collaborators; hidden time; side-effect printing; state not exposed.
  4. How I'd verify: The first test is the failing one: wrong PIN x3 then assert state IDLE and an exception on the 4th call; badPins counted from 1, not 0.
  5. Root cause: ++badPins >= 3 versus badPins++ >= 3 style off-by-one, hidden by no tests.
  6. Fix: Constructor injection of Bank (interface), Dispenser, a LongSupplier clock; a fake bank with in-memory accounts; the ATM exposes state() instead of printing.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
ATM atm = new ATM(new FakeBank(acc), new Dispenser(new Notes(2000,1), new Notes(500,3), new Notes(100,5)));
atm.insertCard("acc1");
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) assertFalse(atm.enterPin("0000"));
assertEquals(AtmState.IDLE, atm.state());          // ejected on the third failure
assertThrows(IllegalStateException.class, () -> atm.enterPin("1234"));
val atm = Atm(mapOf("acc1" to Account("acc1", "1234", 5000)), Dispenser(mutableMapOf(2000 to 1, 500 to 3, 100 to 5)))
atm.insertCard("acc1")
repeat(3) { assertFalse(atm.enterPin("0000")) }
assertEquals(AtmState.IDLE, atm.state)
  1. Prevention: Failure-path matrix: wrong PIN x3, machine lacks notes, insufficient balance, withdraw before login, negative amount, concurrent debit with a latch.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not mock the class under test; not make everything an interface "for testing". Only the bank, dispenser and clock sit at the boundary.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Test the debit/dispense crash? -> Inject a dispenser that throws from commit, assert the journal shows a pending reversal.
  • Real bank calls in CI? -> No; contract tests against a sandbox separately.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An off-by-one in a lockout counter let attackers try four PINs per card for months; the first fix was a test, the second was moving the counter to the bank side.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: mocks statics, tests only happy path.
  • Hire: DI, fake bank, lockout test.
  • Strong hire: injected clock, crash-window test, and failure matrix.

questions.contextHtml:
A customer withdrew 5,000 at an ATM; the screen showed "Out of service", no cash came out, and the SMS says debited. Support sees 212 such cases this week, all during a 14-minute network blip between ATMs and the bank. ATM logs:

12:01:03.100 txn=T91 DEBIT acc7 5000 sent
12:01:08.100 txn=T91 timeout after 5000ms
12:01:08.101 txn=T91 retry DEBIT acc7 5000 sent
12:01:08.140 txn=T91 DEBIT approved
12:01:08.141 dispense plan {2000:2, 500:2} ... machine door jam

Bank side shows two DEBIT rows for acc7 for 5,000 each at 12:01:03.4 and 12:01:08.2.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong, how do you recover customers, and how do you prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Stop retrying." Then timeouts become lost withdrawals, and double-debit risk remains for other paths.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the debit request carry a unique transaction id? Does the bank dedupe on it? Is there an ATM journal and a reversal API?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Run a reconciliation: every debit with no matching "dispensed" journal entry gets reversed; send customers a message; pause retries without ids.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) first debit succeeded but the response was lost, retry debited again (no idempotency key); (b) retry sent a new txn id; (c) jam after debit with no auto-reversal. Red herring: the ATM clock difference.
  4. How I'd verify: Group bank debits by (account, amount, ATM) within 10 seconds; compare with ATM journals; check whether the retry reused T91 (log says yes, so bank-side dedupe is missing).
  5. Root cause: Debit is not idempotent: timeouts mean "unknown", not "failed", and the retry is a second command.
  6. Fix: Bank stores txnId with a unique constraint; a repeat returns the original result. ATM follows with: debit, journal "approved", dispense, journal "dispensed"; if dispense fails it sends a reversal with the same txn id.
  7. Prevention: Daily reconciliation job on unmatched debits; alert when reversal rate rises; chaos test dropping responses.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not remove the retry; I would not trust "no response" as "not done". Reversal needs idempotency too.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Power cut between approve and dispense? -> The journal on disk is replayed on boot and a reversal is sent.
  • Customer disputes with no journal? -> Bank-side trail plus cash-in-cassette audit at the next load.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A flaky link made one retry logic double-charge hundreds of customers; the fix was a unique key per withdrawal, with the unmatched-debit report becoming a daily dashboard.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retry blindly or never.
  • Hire: idempotency key, journal and reversal.
  • Strong hire: explains "timeout means unknown", reconciliation, and idempotent reversal.

questions.contextHtml:
Product adds "transfer between accounts". A developer writes it using the synchronized account from the notes. In load testing the service hangs: 8 threads stuck, none progressing.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amt) {
    synchronized (from) {
        synchronized (to) {
            if (from.debit(amt)) to.credit(amt);
        }
    }
}
// thread 1: transfer(A, B, 10)    thread 2: transfer(B, A, 20)
fun transfer(from: Account, to: Account, amt: Long) {
    synchronized(from) {
        synchronized(to) {
            if (from.debit(amt)) to.credit(amt)
        }
    }
}

A thread dump shows: "Thread-1 waiting to lock B held by Thread-2" and "Thread-2 waiting to lock A held by Thread-1".
questions.promptHtml: Name the problem, fix it, and explain what changes when accounts live in a database.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a timeout." Hides the symptom; or "make one global lock", which kills throughput.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Single JVM or many? Can from == to? Are all transfers within one shard?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart hung nodes; temporarily serialise transfers behind one lock if the outage is live.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) opposite lock order deadlock (confirmed by the dump); (b) self-transfer locking the same object twice (reentrant, harmless in Java but check the logic); (c) lock held during I/O.
  4. How I'd verify: jstack shows the cycle; a test with two threads transferring A to B and B to A 100,000 times each and a latch.
  5. Root cause: Circular wait: each thread holds one lock and wants the other.
  6. Fix: Always lock in a global order, for example by account id: lock the lower id first. Also reject from == to.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amt) {
    if (from == to) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
    Account first = from.id.compareTo(to.id) < 0 ? from : to;
    Account second = first == from ? to : from;
    synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { if (from.debit(amt)) to.credit(amt); } }
}
fun transfer(from: Account, to: Account, amt: Long) {
    require(from !== to)
    val (first, second) = if (from.id < to.id) from to to else to to from
    synchronized(first) { synchronized(second) { if (from.debit(amt)) to.credit(amt) } }
}

With a database: do both updates in one transaction and update rows in id order, or use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE ORDER BY id; the DB also detects deadlocks and aborts one transaction, which you retry. 7. Prevention: Lock-ordering rule in the code review checklist; stress test for opposite-direction transfers; lock timeouts with alerts. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a single global lock (serialises the bank). tryLock with backoff is a fallback, not the primary fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Accounts on different shards? -> No single transaction; use a saga (debit, credit, compensate) with idempotency keys.
  • Equal ids from two sources? -> Tie-break with a stable unique key; ids must be unique.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A month-end batch of mutual transfers froze a service; the dump showed a two-lock cycle, and sorting by id fixed it in ten lines.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: timeout or global lock.
  • Hire: consistent ordering, handles self-transfer.
  • Strong hire: DB transaction/row-lock ordering, deadlock retry, saga for cross-shard.
